ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Psychotic disorders are mental illnesses marked by loss of contact with reality, including delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized thinking. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria and exclusion of medical causes.

b: DSM‑5: ≥1 psychotic symptom >1 month, functional decline
ICD‑11: characteristic psychotic symptoms with duration criteria
sections.p: Psychotic disorders are defined by persistent delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech or behavior, and negative symptoms lasting at least one month, with functional impairment.

b: Prodrome: subthreshold symptoms, functional decline
Acute: full psychosis, may need hospitalization
Residual: persistent negative symptoms, cognitive deficits
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden, functional impairment, and risk of harm. Staging ranges from prodrome (attenuated symptoms) to acute episode to chronic residual phase.

b: Primary schizophrenia spectrum (idiopathic)
Substance‑induced (cannabis, amphetamines)
Infections: HIV, neurosyphilis, TB meningitis, malaria cerebral
Metabolic: severe hyponatremia, hepatic encephalopathy
Autoimmune: anti‑NMDA receptor encephalitis
sections.p: Most cases are idiopathic, but many secondary causes must be ruled out, especially infections and metabolic disorders common in low‑resource settings.

b: Auditory hallucinations are most common
Delusions often persecutory or grandiose
Disorganized speech: loose associations, neologisms
Negative: avolition, anhedonia, alogia
sections.p: Patients may report hearing voices, hold bizarre beliefs, show disorganized speech, or display catatonic behavior. Negative symptoms include flat affect and social withdrawal.
Investigations aim to exclude medical mimics and assess baseline health before treatment.

t.b: Detect anemia, electrolyte disturbances, renal/hepatic dysfunction; abnormal values may explain psychosis or affect medication choice
Identify substance‑induced psychosis; positive result directs withdrawal and specific care

t.a: HIV, syphilis (RPR/TPPA), TB screening (Chest X‑ray, GeneXpert)
t.b: Rule out infectious causes prevalent in low‑resource areas; positive test mandates targeted antimicrobial therapy

t.a: Brain imaging (CT or MRI) if focal deficits or atypical onset
t.b: Detect structural lesions, tumors, or stroke; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam and treat presumptively

t.a: Autoimmune panel (anti‑NMDA receptor antibodies) when rapid onset, seizures, or autonomic instability
t.b: Positive result indicates treatable encephalitis; start immunotherapy

b: Suicidal or homicidal intent
Severe catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk
Rapid deterioration, fever, autonomic instability
Comorbid untreated infection (e.g., TB meningitis)
sections.p: Certain features signal imminent danger or poor prognosis and require urgent intervention.

b: If infection identified → appropriate antimicrobial therapy
First‑line antipsychotic: atypical agents (e.g., risperidone, olanzapine) for efficacy and lower EPS risk
Avoid high‑potency typicals in patients with cardiac disease or seizure risk
Monitor metabolic side effects, QTc, and blood counts
Add psychosocial interventions: CBT for psychosis, family education, occupational therapy
sections.p: Treat underlying cause first, then use antipsychotics for symptom control, plus psychosocial support.

b: Monthly review for first 6 months, then every 3 months
Screen for metabolic syndrome each visit
Educate patient/family on relapse signs and when to seek help
sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, medication side effects, and functional status is essential; relapse prevention focuses on adherence and early warning signs.

b: Severe depression with psychotic features
Bipolar mania with psychosis
Delirium from metabolic or infectious causes
Personality disorder with transient psychotic-like symptoms
sections.p: Several conditions mimic psychosis and must be differentiated.

b: Early HIV serology may be negative; repeat if high suspicion
CSF PCR for TB can be negative; consider clinical picture
Serum electrolytes may appear normal if sampled after aggressive rehydration
sections.p: Certain investigations may be falsely normal, leading to missed diagnoses.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of psychosis with fever or neck stiffness
